slides.title: File System Basics
content: A file system is a structure used by the operating system to organize, store, and retrieve data efficiently on storage devices :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
It manages files, directories, metadata, and permissions to ensure easy access and security
It provides hierarchical organization using folders and subfolders for better data management
It handles operations like file creation, reading, writing, and deletion

slides.title: Types of File Systems
content: FAT32 is a simple and widely compatible file system but has file size limitations and no journaling :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
NTFS is a Windows file system that supports large files, security permissions, encryption, and journaling :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
ext4 is a Linux file system known for performance, reliability, and support for large storage systems :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
APFS is a modern Apple file system optimized for SSDs with features like encryption and snapshots :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

slides.title: File Allocation & Fragmentation
content: File allocation determines how files are stored on disk using methods like contiguous, linked, and indexed allocation
Contiguous allocation stores files in continuous blocks for fast access but causes external fragmentation
Linked allocation stores file blocks as a chain, allowing flexibility but slow random access
Fragmentation occurs when free space becomes scattered, reducing performance and efficient storage usage

slides.title: FCB & ACL
content: A File Control Block (FCB) stores metadata like file name, size, location, permissions, and timestamps for efficient file management :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
Access Control Lists (ACLs) provide detailed permission control for users and groups on files and directories :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
FCB provides basic file information while ACLs provide fine-grained access control
Together they ensure efficient file handling and strong security

slides.title: Authentication & Encryption
content: User authentication verifies identity using passwords, biometrics, or multi-factor authentication to secure system access :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}
Encryption protects file data by converting it into unreadable format using symmetric or asymmetric key techniques :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}
Full-disk encryption secures entire storage while file-level encryption protects specific files
These mechanisms ensure data confidentiality, integrity, and protection from unauthorized access

slides.title: Journaling & Backup
content: Journaling file systems record changes in a log before applying them to prevent data corruption during crashes
It ensures quick recovery by replaying journal entries to restore consistency
Backup mechanisms store copies of data using full, incremental, or differential methods for recovery
Recovery techniques restore data after failures, ensuring data safety and system reliability :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}
